newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Market takes Astra profit rise in stride.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Market takes Astra profit rise in stride.

text.p: Sweden's largest company Astra AB on Monday posted a slight lift in profits for the first nine months of 1996, but the rise was widely expected and the news failed to inject any enthusiasm into the market.
Astra reported an eight precent rise in pre-tax profit to 9.85 billion crowns ($1.5 billion) in the period to September 30 against market expectations of 9.81 billion crowns.
"It was a good, solid report with no great surprises," analyst James McKean of Morgan Stanley told Reuters.
Astra's shares, which account for 12 percent of the market capitalisation on the Stockholm bourse, slipped on the result, trading one crown lower at 301 at 1515 GMT.
"This really was just a reaction to the fact it was a set of numbers very hard to say anything about," McKean said.
Sales rose two percent in Astra's key European markets and 19 percent in North America, giving an overall rise of five percent to 28.14 billion crowns.

But Astra said the stronger crown made comparisons with 1995 less flattering. After hedging, the stronger crown wiped 600 million crowns off results in the first six months of the year and another 150 million in the third quarter.
"Calculated at constant exchange rates, sales growth was 16 percent which is the same growth as in the first half of the year," Astra said in the report.
The crown was expected to have negative impact of another 150 million crowns in the fourth quarter.
Once again, Astra was able to report higher sales for its leading drug, the antipeptic ulcer agent Losec, with worldwide turnover increasing to 17.78 billion crowns compared to 15.55 billion.
This included sales in the U.S. where Astra markets Losec in conjunction with Merck Inc through joint venture vehicle Astra Merck.
Astra's share of Losec sales rose 12 percent to 12.74 billion crowns -- or 22 percent at constant exchange rates.
President Hakan Mogren told Reuters that there was still plenty of scope for Losec sales to expand further.
"Losec has not been on the U.S. market very long, the growth rate there is around 40 percent," Mogren said.
He said broader approvals for use of the drug in Japan in late 1997 or early 1998 would also help maintain sales growth.
Sales of Astra's second largest drug, the anti-asthma agent Pulmicort, edged up three percent to 3.32 billion crowns.
Astra said its beta-blocker Seloken in the cardiovascular group, was showing rapid growth, rising four percent to 1.87 billion crowns, or 17 percent at constant exchange rates.
"This was mainly due to a favourable trend in the U.S. where the product has been marketed since 1992 under the name Toprol-XL," the company said.
Sales of pain controllers rose three percent at constant exchange rates, or fell eight percent in crowns, to 2.40 billion crowns.
"The only disappointment really was pain control, analgesics and anesthetics which could have been better," analyst Janet Dyson of Merrill Lynch told Reuters.
Analyst John Reeve from Paribas said Astra was on track to meet its target of spending seven billion crowns on research and development (R&D) in 1996, if not more.
He said an R&D conference in London and New York later this year would attract some interest.
Mogren said: "Our ambition is to continue growing from this (R&D) base by around 20 percent per year in expenditure terms. If we see more opportunities then we'll add something more to that."
($1=6.58 crowns)
